title: Panna Cotta
subtitle: vanilla set cream dessert
excerpt: Panna Cotta is a silky Italian dessert made by warming cream with sugar and vanilla, then setting it gently with gelatine and chilling until just firm. It unmoulds onto a plate as a smooth, quivering dome and needs no more than a spoonful of fruit alongside. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Panna Cotta is a dessert from Piedmont in northern Italy. The name means 'cooked cream' and the dish is thought to have been made in the region since at least the early 20th century. It became internationally known in the 1990s and is now one of Italy's most copied desserts.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the day before and chill overnight.

content.text: is one of the simplest Italian desserts to make: cream, sugar, vanilla and

are warmed together, poured into moulds and chilled until set. The texture should be just barely firm, soft enough that the dessert quivers when you tap the mould. This recipe serves 4 and the hands-on time is only 15 minutes.

Getting the gelatine ratio right is the main thing to watch. Too little and the panna cotta will not unmould cleanly; too much and it will be rubbery. The quantities here give a soft, barely-set result that collapses slightly as it hits the plate, which is exactly right.
Soak the gelatine leaves in a bowl of cold water for 5 minutes until soft and floppy.

Combine the cream, milk and caster sugar in a medium saucepan. Warm over medium-low heat, stirring occasionally, until the sugar dissolves and the mixture is just below the boil. Remove from the heat and stir in the vanilla extract.
Lift the gelatine sheets from the water and squeeze out any excess. Add them to the warm cream mixture and stir until completely dissolved.
Lightly oil four ramekins or dariole moulds with a neutral-flavoured oil. Pour the cream mixture through a fine sieve into a jug, then divide between the moulds.
Leave to cool for 15 minutes at room temperature, then cover each mould with cling film and refrigerate for at least 4 hours until fully set.

To unmould, run a thin knife around the edge of each mould. Place a dessert plate face-down on top, then invert quickly. Give the mould a sharp tap and lift away. Serve with fresh fruit or a drizzle of balsamic reduction.

attrs.symptom: Panna cotta will not come out of the mould in one piece
attrs.cause: Either the mould was not oiled or the dessert was not set firmly enough
attrs.fix: Oil the moulds lightly before filling and chill for at least 4 hours; run a knife carefully around the edge before inverting

attrs.symptom: Texture is rubbery and bounces on the plate
attrs.cause: Too much gelatine or sheets were not squeezed out before adding
attrs.fix: Use exactly 3 sheets of gelatine for this quantity of cream and milk, and always squeeze out the water thoroughly first

attrs.symptom: Cream mixture has lumps or strings of gelatine
attrs.cause: Gelatine was added before the cream was warm enough to melt it
attrs.fix: Make sure the cream is hot (just below boiling) before adding the squeezed gelatine sheets, and stir until fully dissolved

content.text: Panna cotta is served in trattorie across northern Italy, usually with a spoonful of fruit coulis or a drizzle of honey. In Piedmont it often comes with a dark balsamic reduction. It is one of the few restaurant desserts that translates perfectly to a home kitchen without any specialist equipment. It also improves with time in the fridge, which makes it suited to cooking ahead.
